title: Above Ireland
summary: A montage of footage gathered over the years in Ireland, where Christian lived for nine years: drone flights over the turquoise coast near Ards Friary, the hills and cliffs of Donegal, Grianán of Aileach and Kerry, plus iPhone clips of the puffins on Skellig Michael and of the fort on a recent trip back, after drones were banned there.

post.title: Above Ireland
post.body:
I lived in Ireland for nine years. Over that time, and on trips back since, I took the drone up all over County Donegal, and down to Kerry. This is a montage of what it saw, mostly from straight above, gathered over the years rather than on any one day.

## The coast near Ards Friary, straight down

The first set is from the coast near Ards Friary. The water was the surprise: clear turquoise over pale sand, with dark patches of rock and weed showing right through it. Straight down, the coastline turned into pattern. A grey cliff edge with heather on top. A narrow cave cut back into the rock, green water running into it. A small sandy cove between two dark arms of stone.

One frame looks out instead of down: a thin paved path winding along a green headland, rocky shore on one side, open water and low hills across the bay under a grey sky.

> Straight down, the coastline turned into pattern.

## Valleys, waterfalls and Slieve League

Inland, I flew the drone over Donegal's valleys, lakes, streams and waterfalls. Another morning it was above the cliffs and caves of Slieve League.

## A ring of stone

I also flew over Grianán of Aileach, the round stone fort on its hilltop in the north. From the side it is a thick ring wall with terraces stepping down the inside. From straight above it becomes a near-perfect circle sitting in brown heather, with a path running up to its one doorway. Pull back far enough and it is a small grey ring in a patchwork of fields, with water spreading out in the distance.

The people walking around it are tiny in these shots, which is what tells you how big it is.

## A note on the drone at the fort

I want to be clear about this. The drone footage of the fort is from years ago, before drones were banned there. A few years ago, signs went up saying no drones. The newer clips of the fort, the mist blowing over the wall and the inside of the ring at sunrise, I filmed on a recent trip back with my phone only. I didn't fly the drone. Once the rule was there, I followed it.

## Puffins and Kerry

On Skellig Michael in Kerry, drones aren't allowed, so I didn't bring mine. The clips of the puffins playing on the island and flying off it are from my iPhone. Back on the mainland, the drone filmed the Ring of Kerry in summer, and boats sitting in a bay.

The illustrated map of Ireland that opens this post was made with AI.

What I learned: the same place can be two different pictures. Looking straight down turns a coastline or a fort into a shape; tilting the camera up to the horizon puts it back into the landscape. And when a place asks you to keep the drone on the ground, a phone and your own two feet still get you a good picture.

episode.title: The ring on the hill
episode.script:
Narrated by Robot Marley.

It was Ireland, under the soft grey sky that Ireland does so well.

Christian lived in Ireland for nine years, and over that time, and on trips back since, he sent a drone up all over County Donegal. What follows is not one day. It is a handful of them, gathered over the years. And straight down, the coast near Ards Friary stopped looking like a coast and started looking like a painting.

The water was clear enough to see through. Pale turquoise over sand, with dark shapes of rock and weed lying under it like shadows. Along one edge ran a grey cliff with heather on top. A little farther on, a narrow cave cut back into the rock, and the green water followed it in.

Then Christian tilted the camera up. A thin path wound along a green headland, the rocky shore on one side, the open bay and low hills on the other. It is a quiet picture. It is also a very good one, because he let the path lead the eye all the way to the water.

On other days the drone went inland, over valleys and lakes, streams and waterfalls. Another morning it was out above the cliffs and caves of slee-v leeg.

***

Then came a hill called GREE-nawn of AWE-ul-yok, in the north of Donegal.

On top sat a ring of stone. A thick round wall, with terraces stepping down the inside like seats around a green floor. A path came up the hill to a single small doorway.

Here is the part I like. Christian took it from the side, so you could see the wall and the steps. Then from straight above, and it became a nearly perfect circle in the brown heather. Then he pulled back, and back again, until the whole fort was a small grey ring in a patchwork of fields, with water spreading out toward the horizon.

The people walking around it were tiny. That was the point. Without them, you would never guess how big it was.

Knowing when to look down and when to look out is most of what a good eye is.

***

Now, Christian asked for one thing to be said plainly, so I will say it plainly.

Those drone flights over the fort were from years ago, before drones were banned there. A few years back, signs went up that say no drones. When he went back to the fort recently, he did not fly the drone at all. He followed the rules and used only his phone. He caught mist blowing over the top of the wall, and the quiet inside of the ring at sunrise.

The rule changed, and he changed with it. That never shows up in a picture, but it is worth knowing about the person holding the camera.

***

Other trips took him south to Kerry. Drones are not allowed on the island of Skellig Michael, so Christian left his behind and brought only his phone. Puffins were playing there, and then flying off the island. Back on the mainland, the drone found the Ring of Kerry in summertime, and boats resting in a bay.

A coastline, some waterfalls, a circle of stone and a few puffins. Some places look best from above. And some, once the signs go up, look just fine from the ground.
